original_question: Determine whether there exists a discrete group Γ that is both residually finite and residually soluble, so that the canonical maps Γ -> PF(Γ) and Γ -> PS(Γ) are injective, but for which the canonical map Γ -> PFS(Γ) to the prosoluble completion built from finite soluble quotients is not injective.
target_in_paper: Section 6, item (6.G): the open problem asking whether there exists a discrete group Gamma for which the canonical maps Gamma -> P_F(Gamma) and Gamma -> P_S(Gamma) are injective, while the canonical map Gamma -> P_FS(Gamma) is not injective.
correct_elements: Your draft matches the paper's target almost verbatim. It correctly asks an existence question about a discrete group, correctly identifies the two residual properties through injectivity of the canonical maps to the profinite completion P_F(Gamma) and the true prosoluble completion P_S(Gamma), and correctly asks for failure of injectivity of the canonical map to P_FS(Gamma), the completion built from finite soluble quotients.
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, define F as the family of all normal subgroups of finite index in Gamma, so that P_F(Gamma) is the profinite completion.
Define S as the family of all normal subgroups N normal in Gamma such that Gamma/N is soluble, so that P_S(Gamma) is the true prosoluble completion.

Define FS as the family of all normal subgroups N normal in Gamma such that Gamma/N is finite and soluble, so that P_FS(Gamma) is the inverse limit over finite soluble quotients; the paper stresses that this is the usual 'prosoluble completion' of the literature and is different from the true prosoluble completion.
If one wants the statement to mirror the paper's notation exactly, the three maps should be named phi_F, phi_S, and phi_FS.
It helps to state explicitly that item (6.G) imposes no extra hypotheses such as finite generation or finite presentation.

By Section 2(A), noninjectivity of Gamma -> P_FS(Gamma) is equivalent to saying that the intersection of all normal subgroups with finite soluble quotient is nontrivial; this equivalent kernel formulation is implicit in your draft.
refined_question: Does there exist a discrete group Gamma such that the canonical homomorphism phi_F: Gamma -> P_F(Gamma), where P_F(Gamma) is the profinite completion with respect to all normal subgroups of finite index, is injective, and the canonical homomorphism phi_S: Gamma -> P_S(Gamma), where P_S(Gamma) is the true prosoluble completion with respect to all normal subgroups N normal in Gamma for which Gamma/N is soluble, is injective, but the canonical homomorphism phi_FS: Gamma -> P_FS(Gamma), where P_FS(Gamma) is the inverse limit over all finite soluble quotients Gamma/N, is not injective?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, does there exist a discrete group Gamma such that the intersection of all finite-index normal subgroups of Gamma is {1}, and the intersection of all normal subgroups N with soluble quotient Gamma/N is {1}, but the intersection of all normal subgroups N with Gamma/N finite and soluble is nontrivial?
justification: The draft is targeting the open problem stated explicitly in Section 6 as item (6.G), not Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3. The introduction defines residual finiteness and residual solubility through injectivity of the canonical maps to P_F(Gamma) and P_S(Gamma). Section 4(A) defines P_F, while Section 4(B) defines the true prosoluble completion P_S and distinguishes it from P_FS, the completion built from finite soluble quotients. Section 2(A) states that for any directed family N of normal subgroups, the canonical map into P_N has kernel equal to the intersection of that family, which yields the equivalent intersection formulation. Nearby examples (6.A) and (6.B) explain that the relation between P_S and P_FS can fail in both surjectivity and injectivity, so item (6.G) is the precise sharper existence question your draft is capturing.
